title: Warehouse and distributed-platform migrations
summary: Assess Cinderline's three estates: inventory by readers, segment into dispositions, bridge cut dependencies, profile each source platform in its vendor's words, separate silent differences from loud ones, and sequence waves from pilot to rollback.
objectives: Inventory an estate by readers, give each workload one disposition, driver and evidence, and bridge every dependency a wave cuts.
Profile legacy, Hadoop and cloud warehouse sources from their vendors' own documentation and classify dialect and engine differences as loud or silent.
Prove results, performance and permissions separately, set reconciliation depth by risk class, and write a pilot-to-rollback sequence with checkable tests.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
Each source platform in its own vendor's terms
Security models, data movement and BI continuity
Waves, coexistence and the pilot-to-rollback sequence
What the Harrowmere assessment must show

questions.prompt: Which Cinderline workload meets all five pilot criteria: bounded, representative of a hard feature, a reconciliation basis, an available owner and a reversible read path?

options.text: The plant-quality mart: it can start with one plant, uses the dialect features the rest of Basalt shares, has Basalt reports to reconcile against, a named owner and a read path that can switch back.
options.rationale: All five criteria hold, and the old reports keep running while it is tested.

options.text: The finance close marts, because they are the most valuable and so prove the most.
options.rationale: They sit behind the year-end blackout at class 1 risk; a pilot needs a reversible, bounded slice, not the highest stakes.

options.text: The sensor rollup job, because it is small and purely technical.
options.rationale: Its output feeds dashboards across platforms and its engine upgrade is untested, so it belongs to wave 2.

options.text: The supplier extract, because it runs every day.
options.rationale: A contract fixes its format, and the supplier, not Cinderline, would have to accept any change.

questions.prompt: Which evidence shows that the target grants the same access as Basalt did?

options.text: A persona test: the same queries run as each persona on both paths, comparing allowed or denied, row counts and masked values.
options.rationale: Only outcomes show what each persona can see, including widening through inheritance or a dropped view.

options.text: Every translated GRANT statement ran without error.
options.rationale: A grant that compiles can still widen access, for example through a parent grant that reaches future tables.

options.text: The groups have the same names on both platforms.
options.rationale: Names say nothing about membership, inheritance or the row and column policies applied.

options.text: The conversion report lists no security warnings.
options.rationale: Conversion tools check syntax, not the outcomes each persona actually sees.

questions.prompt: Pellworth's warehouse will be down overnight during month-end. Which data movement option keeps the 06:00 close supplied with Pellworth figures?

options.text: A nightly incremental copy into the lakehouse after Pellworth's month-end run, labelled with its as-of time.
options.rationale: A copy decouples readers from source downtime; it lags the source but is available at 06:00.
Federation reads the source in place, so it fails while the source is down.

options.text: Both federation and a copy, merged at query time.
options.rationale: Two sources for one dataset break the one-writer rule and make reconciliation ambiguous.

options.text: A sync-back from the lakehouse into Pellworth's warehouse.
options.rationale: A sync-back flows toward the old platform; it does not bring Pellworth's figures to the lakehouse.

cards.prompt: Why join the catalog to query history before sizing a warehouse migration?
cards.answer: Because the catalog only counts objects, while usage shows which are read by people, only by scripts, or by nobody.
cards.explanation: Basalt's catalog listed 1,240 tables. Joined to 90 days of query history, 610 had people or reports reading them, 410 were read only by scheduled scripts and 220 had no reader. The first group is work with consumers, the second moves with its producers and the third becomes retirement candidates for owners to confirm.

cards.prompt: Name two kinds of reader a query log can miss during an inventory.
cards.answer: Dynamic SQL that builds table names at run time, and extracts copied to desktops or other systems.
cards.explanation: A query log records the statements a platform ran. Dynamic SQL names its tables only at execution and an extract is read later somewhere else, so both can look unread; annual jobs outside the window are a third gap. List each as a named gap with an owner, because an unknown reader is not the same as no reader.

cards.prompt: What makes 'not yet' a legitimate disposition rather than a delay?
cards.answer: A specific, dated and owned condition for reconsidering it, plus the evidence it will need then.
cards.explanation: Cinderline's finance close marts are 'not yet' because the year-end close is a blackout. They are reconsidered on 15 February with the finance owner's sign-off and one full close run in parallel as the evidence. Without the date and the owner, 'not yet' would just be an unplanned delay nobody is accountable for.

cards.prompt: What is a cut dependency in a wave plan, and what must accompany it?
cards.answer: An edge whose two ends move in different waves; it needs a bridge with an owner, a direction and an end date.
cards.explanation: Once the earlier wave cuts over, one end of the edge runs on the target and the other on the source. A forward bridge lets a moved consumer read an unmoved producer; a backward bridge, or sync-back, feeds a consumer left behind. Either can become permanent by accident unless its end date is written into the plan.

cards.prompt: What should a platform profile cell hold if nobody has read the vendor's current page?
cards.answer: The word unknown, an owner and the page to read, never a value recalled from memory.
cards.explanation: The profile's source side decides every later mapping, so a remembered value carries errors silently. Microsoft's Fabric overview, for example, says the warehouse stores Delta Lake tables in OneLake but names no SQL dialect for it, so that cell stays unknown until someone reads the warehouse's own reference.

cards.prompt: Which four things move on separate tracks when a Hadoop estate migrates?
cards.answer: The files, the table metadata, the engine version that runs the jobs, and the permission model that guards data.
cards.explanation: HDFS files are copied to object storage; the Hive metastore's names and paths are registered in Unity Catalog or federated for a while; Spark 2.4 jobs rerun on a current runtime with documented behaviour changes; directory permissions are re-expressed as table grants. Schedules are a simpler fifth track rebuilt as jobs.

cards.prompt: Why is integer division riskier than an unsupported function during a warehouse migration?
cards.answer: It compiles and runs on both engines but returns a different value, so only keyed value checks catch it.
cards.explanation: An unsupported function fails at compile time and gets fixed before anything is published. Basalt truncates 7 / 2 to 3, but Spark documents that its / always performs floating point division and returns 3.5. Row counts match and nothing errors, so the change surfaces only when keyed values are compared or a reader notices a number move.

cards.prompt: What does '92.6 percent converted' tell a steering group about a migration?
cards.answer: Only that 389 of 420 scripts parsed and produced target SQL; it proves nothing about equivalence.
cards.explanation: Conversion measures syntax. Results need keyed reconciliation, performance needs a replay of recorded queries against a target, and permissions need persona outcome tests. In Cinderline's pilot, five of the 38 converted scripts still returned different keyed values, two dashboards missed their response target and one grant widened access.

cards.prompt: Before recommending Lakebridge, which status labels does release 0.15.2 carry?
cards.answer: Databricks Labs, a Beta classifier, exploration-only and AS-IS support wording, and experimental reconcile commands.
cards.explanation: These labels come from the package itself: the PyPI classifier Development Status 4 - Beta, the README's Project Support section saying it is not formally supported with service level agreements, and the command help marking reconcile and aggregates-reconcile experimental. Quote the labels of the release actually in use and plan for work that no support agreement covers.

cards.prompt: Why can a translated schema grant widen access compared with per-table grants?
cards.answer: In Unity Catalog a parent grant can reach current and future tables, which per-table source grants never did.
cards.explanation: Basalt granted the contractor group SELECT table by table. Reproducing that as one schema-level grant looks equivalent on the day of translation, but a table created next week inherits it. Only a persona outcome test that includes a newly created table exposes the difference before a contractor finds it.

cards.prompt: How does a federated dataset behave differently from a copied one when its source is down?
cards.answer: Federated queries fail with the source; a copy stays readable but stale until its next load.
cards.explanation: Federation reads in place and is read-only, so every query needs the source's availability and capacity. A copy decouples readers from the source at the cost of lag. Choose per dataset by what its consumers tolerate: a close that needs Pellworth figures at 06:00 during maintenance needs a copy.

cards.prompt: Besides the connection, what must move with a report to keep its numbers?
cards.answer: Its measures, the business rules hidden in source views, its refresh schedule and the identity it runs as.
cards.explanation: Cinderline's plant dashboard changed on 3 of 30 days after a repoint because the 06:00 cutoff and the test-lot exclusion lived in Basalt's view. Moving both into one governed definition, refreshing after the pipeline completes and running as a named service principal restored parity per plant and day.

cards.prompt: What sets a workload's reconciliation risk class, and when is it set?
cards.answer: The consequence of a wrong number, decided before the first comparison runs.
cards.explanation: Finance close marts are class 1, the plant-quality mart class 2 and exploration tables class 3. Every class still writes the basis and compares every key; the class changes field coverage, tolerances, parallel-run length, performance and permission depth, and who signs. Choosing after results lets differences lower their own bar.

cards.prompt: Why order migration waves by dependencies rather than by size?
cards.answer: Because size ignores cut dependencies and fixed blackouts, which decide what can safely move first.
cards.explanation: Moving Cinderline's largest estate, the sensor cluster, first would leave dashboards reading line_health across platforms and push finance into the year-end blackout. Ordering foundations, then the pilot, producers before consumers and finance after the fixed blackout keeps bridges few and every wave's exit test reachable.

cards.prompt: What does the one-writer rule forbid during a parallel run?
cards.answer: Editing the new copy directly: corrections go through the old path, which writes until cutover.
cards.explanation: During the parallel run Basalt is the authoritative writer and the lakehouse copy is derived and compared. An edit to the copy creates a second writer, so the next comparison reports a difference that is not a migration defect. After cutover the writer flips, and any sync-back to Basalt is read-only.

cards.prompt: What distinguishes a parallel run from a pilot?
cards.answer: A pilot proves a bounded slice; a parallel run compares the whole wave daily until its clean-day count is met.
cards.explanation: Both keep users on the old path. The pilot's exit is keyed reconciliation and persona tests for one plant plus the owner's acceptance; the parallel run's exit is the class's count of consecutive clean days for all plants, a performance replay and a rehearsed rollback. Any fix restarts the count.
